newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-EU seeks WTO panel on U.S. anti-Cuba law.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU seeks WTO panel on U.S. anti-Cuba law.

text.p: The European Union on Friday moved formally to achieve creation of a World Trade Organisation panel on the U.S. Helms-Burton Cuban investment law which Brussels argues violates trade rules, a senior EU official said.

The official, acting head of the EU Geneva mission Ian Wilkinson, told Reuters the request for a panel had been forwarded to the WTO for inclusion on the agenda of a meeting on October 16 of the organisation's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB).

EU foreign ministers decided earlier this week to press ahead with the case in the WTO despite a major diplomatic effort by Washington to keep the potentially explosive dispute out of the fledgling trade body.

The United States is almost certain to block creation of a panel on October 16, as permitted under DSB rules, but if the EU renews the request as expected at the body's next meeting, the panel would be set up automatically.
But the panel process, with appeals, can take well over a year, although an initial finding would be handed down within six months.

The Helms-Burton law, which has been condemned by all major U.S. trading partners, including Canada and Mexico, allows U.S. citizens to sue foreign firms who invest in property confiscated after the 1959 Cuban revolution.

Washington argues that the issue is a matter of national security, covered by an untested provision of long-existing world trade rules which allows any WTO member to suspend operation of overall trade agreements.

Many trade diplomats fear that trying out the provision -- article 21 of the WTO's underlying accord, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, or GATT -- could put the entire structure of world trade rules at risk.

If a panel found against the EU, they argue, it could open the way for any country when it saw fit to abandon WTO commitments to open trading by claiming it was acting in defence of "national security."

At the same time, this argument runs, if the panel process ended with a finding against Washington on such a highly- emotive issue, it could seriously undermine already precarious support in the United States for membership of the WTO.

Canada and Mexico, whose trading links with Fidel Castro's Cuba are also seriously affected by the Helms-Burton law, have so far preferred to tackle Washington in the framework of their North American Free Trade Agreement, NAFTA.
But they, like the EU, are preparing laws to enable their own firms to countersue in their courts any U.S. company which sought and won cases against them in the United States.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky made clear earlier this week Washington would firmly defend its position in the WTO. The Helms-Burton law, she said, "is absolutely consistent with our international obgliations."

President Bill Clinton, who approved the bill named after its two Congressional sponsors in the wake of the downing by Cuba in January of two planes flown by anti-Castro exiles, has suspended part of the bill allowing lawsuits.
But he has called on other powers to show commitment to promoting democracy in Cuba, saying this would be a factor when he decides in January whether to suspend the provision again.

However, Washington has gone ahead with other action under the law barring executives of major firms operating in Cuba and their families from the United States. The EU, Canada and Mexico are considering counter-action on this front also.
